rounds.text: Highway Infrastructure Ltd is fundamentally undervalued and supported by a compelling margin of safety, as a discounted cash flow model establishes an intrinsic value of Rs 148 per share against the current market price of Rs 85.1 [E39, E40]. This valuation gap is further reinforced by a reverse DCF showing that the market price only prices in a modest 10.4% earnings growth compared to the 18.0% growth assumed in the base case [E41]. The business demonstrates exceptional operational efficiency and profitability, outperforming sector benchmarks with a robust return on capital employed of 18.8% and a median return on equity of 18% to 19% over recent years [E12, E21, E22, E23]. Top-line expansion is exceptionally strong, backed by a compounded sales growth of 33% over 5 years and an impressive 93% surge over the trailing twelve months [E14, E16]. These fundamentals are complemented by a strong macroeconomic tailwind in the services sector, which carries a tailwind score of +0.64 and robust rules-based screen support of 87 out of 100 [E58, E65, E67]. conceded: [E28] and [E30].

The valuation of Highway Infrastructure Ltd carries significant risks because key multiples outpace sector benchmarks, with a P/E of 23.67x compared to the sector at 18.61x, and a P/B of 2.55x against a sector benchmark of 1.33x [E6, E7]. This premium valuation rests on shaky fundamental delivery, highlighted by a -19% drop in compounded profit growth over the trailing twelve months and a long-term yearly operating-margin trend that has been decreasing over the last four years [E19, E26]. Furthermore, cash generation has completely disconnected from reported profits, resulting in a severe cash conversion of -2.06x alongside a negative operating cash flow of Rs -66 Cr and negative free cash flow of Rs -74 Cr in March 2026 [E28, E29, E30]. Operational efficiency is also deteriorating as debtor days stretched from 28.5 to 38.9 days and working capital days ballooned from 53.6 to 78.2 days [E56, E57]. Institutional investors are actively fleeing these deteriorating metrics, demonstrated by domestic institutional holdings dropping from 2.01% to 0.39% and scanX flagging a negative money flow signal [E37, E38]. Conceded: the company boasts robust 5-year and 3-year compounded sales growth of 33% and 32% respectively, alongside strong medium-term return on equity figures and an impressive relative-strength rating of 100 [E14, E15, E21, E22, E45].

Conceded: P/E sits at 23.67x against a sector benchmark of 18.61x and P/B is 2.55x against 1.33x [E6, E7]. However, this premium is fully justified by superior capital efficiency, as the company delivers an impressive ROCE of 18.8% and ROE of 18.8%, dramatically outperforming sector medians of 6.9% and 18.2% respectively [E12, E13, E68, E70]. Conceded: TTM profit growth dipped -19% [E19]. Nevertheless, this ignores explosive top-line acceleration where compounded sales growth reached 93% over the trailing twelve months and quarterly operating margin rebounded by 11 percentage points year-over-year in September 2026 [E16, E25]. Conceded: operating cash flow was Rs -66 Cr in March 2026 [E29]. Yet the balance sheet maintains a comfortable short-term current ratio of 2.09x alongside moderate leverage of 0.52x, supported by strong sector tailwinds scoring +0.64 [E31, E32, E65].

Conceded: the company maintains a current ratio of 2.09x and moderate leverage of 0.52x [E31, E32]. However, the bull’s reliance on ROCE and ROE ignores the critical reality that the company is burning cash, with operating cash flow at Rs -66 Cr and free cash flow at Rs -74 Cr in March 2026 [E29, E30]. While the bull highlights top-line growth, it fails to address that this expansion is failing to translate into bottom-line stability, evidenced by a -19% drop in TTM profit growth and a long-term decreasing trend in operating margins [E19, E26]. The bull’s focus on superior capital efficiency is undermined by the fact that cash conversion is a deeply negative -2.06x, suggesting that reported profits are not being backed by actual cash generation [E28]. Furthermore, the bull ignores the deteriorating working capital cycle, as debtor days have climbed to 38.9 and total working capital days have ballooned to 78.2 [E56, E57]. Finally, the premium valuation is increasingly difficult to justify given that institutional investors are actively reducing their stake, resulting in a negative money flow signal [E37, E38].
